anchors.fact: In 1886 four men named Nix imported tomatoes from the West Indies into New York and paid the 10% duty on vegetables, under protest, because fruit came in free, and sued to get it back. In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled that botanically the tomato is the fruit of a vine, like cucumbers, beans and peas, but that in the everyday speech of the people who buy and sell food it's a vegetable, so for the tariff it was taxed as one.
anchors.meaning: The Court saw both and picked the dinner table's word, for a tax. Nobody was wronged and nothing was misfiled by mistake; the everyday name won over the botanical one, for a tax, the way it usually does. **Not a horoscope** (Wren): the guest isn't the misfiled tomato.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: At trial both sides read dictionary definitions into evidence (the importers: "fruit", "vegetables", "tomato"; the collector: pea, egg plant, cucumber, squash, pepper), and two witnesses who'd sold fruit and vegetables for thirty years gave evidence.
anchors.meaning: Everyone reached for the book. *I like to think* the guest would have skipped the dictionaries and served it for dessert (Wren's sideways leap; our reading, signposted, never history).

anchors.fact: The Court's reason was where it's eaten: tomatoes are served with or after the soup, fish or meat, not like fruit, as dessert.
anchors.meaning: Where a thing sat at dinner decided what it was called. The glass simply moves it to the other seat: say what you see before anyone rules on it.

anchors.fact: Botanically a berry is a fruit that encloses its seeds. By that definition the tomato is a berry; the strawberry isn't (it's an aggregate fruit).
anchors.meaning: The fact that sounds made up and is true: the guest's "this is going to sound weird, but…", correct a minute later. Always "botanically".

anchors.fact: *The Flavor Matrix* lists strawberries as a substitute for tomato (pdf 244) and tomato as one of vanilla's surprise pairings (pdf 256). Here cherry tomatoes are crushed with sugar and a split vanilla pod into a syrup, made the way the *Cocktail Codex* makes its cold-blended strawberry syrup (equal weights of fruit and sugar, blended, sieved, p. 47), tomatoes in the strawberries' place, and shaken into a daiquiri (rum, lime, syrup; pp. 105–106).
anchors.meaning: Tomás's build, not a historical recipe. The strangeness is in the recipe, not in a trick: it tastes of ripe red fruit and vanilla before it tastes of an idea. Served straight-faced, like the guest's odd remark.

cocktail.closingLine: Tell them it's tomato before they taste it.
method: A day ahead, make the syrup (above).
Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the rum, the lime juice and the syrup into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Empty the glass if it's full of ice water. Strain the drink into it through a small sieve, so no bits of tomato get through.
Cut a small slit in the bottom of a cherry tomato and sit it on the rim, where the strawberry would go.
cocktail.name: The Other Berry

preparations.text: (a day ahead; makes enough for a dozen drinks or more): put 250 g ripe cherry tomatoes and 250 g white sugar in a blender and blend until completely smooth and the sugar has dissolved. Don't heat it. Push it through a fine sieve into a jar, pressing the pulp to get all the liquid out, and throw the skins and seeds away. Split a vanilla pod lengthways, scrape the seeds into the jar and drop the pod in. Leave it in the fridge overnight, then take the pod out. It keeps up to two weeks in the fridge. Taste it before you use it, and if it fizzes at all, throw it out. (No pod? Half a teaspoon of vanilla extract instead.)
preparations.title: Cherry-tomato and vanilla syrup

cocktail.tagline: You don't make things strange. You notice they already are.

reading.epigraph: Made like a strawberry daiquiri. There isn't a strawberry in it.
whoYouAre: You've started a hundred sentences with "this is going to sound weird, but…". Then you say what you saw: the thing that looks like something else, two ideas nobody thought belonged together. There's a pause, then a laugh. About a minute later, it doesn't sound weird at all.

None of it is a performance. You're just saying what's there. You laugh along, but you meant it, and it stings a little when it's taken as only a joke. So the strangest things you see, you mostly don't say. What you can't stand is the sensible version: an idea sanded down until it fits in. What you give people is a second look at things they thought they knew.
yours: In 1886, four men named Nix brought tomatoes into New York from the West Indies. They paid the tax on vegetables, under protest, because fruit came in free, and sued to get the money back. At the trial, both sides read dictionaries aloud. The importers looked up "fruit", "vegetables" and "tomato"; the other side looked up "pea", "cucumber" and "squash". Two men who'd sold produce for thirty years gave evidence.

The case reached the US Supreme Court, and in 1893 it answered. Botanically, the Court said, the tomato is the fruit of a vine. But the people who buy and sell food call it a vegetable, because it's served with the soup, the fish or the meat, not as dessert. So for the tariff, it was a vegetable. And botany goes further than the Court did: the tomato is, botanically, a berry. The strawberry isn't.

My guess is you'd have skipped the dictionaries. You'd have looked at it, red, its seeds kept on the inside the way a berry keeps them, and served it for dessert. It's what you do with everything: you go by what a thing is, not by where it usually sits.

So this is a daiquiri (rum, lime and sugar, shaken), made the way you'd make a strawberry one, with the tomato in the strawberry's seat. The syrup is made the way a strawberry syrup is: ripe cherry tomatoes blended cold with sugar, plus a vanilla pod, because vanilla and tomato, surprisingly, go well together. It tastes of ripe red fruit and vanilla first, and only then of an idea. There's no trick in it. It's the tomato, served where it looked like it belonged.

You apologise in advance for things you'll turn out to be right about. Drop the "this is going to sound weird". It gives people a way to laugh it off before they've looked. Say what you saw, plainly, the first time. Then let them catch up. They usually do, about a minute later.
